script.opening: (In his lorry cab on a break, looking at his watch.) "Morning doc. Look, I know it's a review, but honestly I just need my omeprazole renewed — I've been on it for years, it works, I don't want a big song and dance about it. Can we just sort the repeat so I can get back on the road? I've got a delivery window."

facts.text: "Heartburn, years back. Another doctor started it." About eight years ago. Never had a camera test or a breath or stool test for H. pylori. "It's mostly fine now" — the odd bit of heartburn after a big curry.

Pause: "…Funny you ask. The last few weeks, bread and meat sometimes feel like they stick. I just take smaller bites. It's nothing." About six weeks. "Mostly solids. Maybe a bit worse. Drinks are fine." Points to the lower breastbone. No pain on swallowing.
"Trousers are a bit looser. I've not weighed myself. I hadn't really thought about it." Has had to tighten his belt a notch over two months. Appetite a bit less.
If asked: "No. None of that" — no vomiting, no vomiting blood, no black stools, no upper tummy pain or lump, no hoarse voice, no cough with food.
Omeprazole 20 mg once a day. Occasional ibuprofen for his back, "once a fortnight maybe". No aspirin. No allergies.
Long-distance lorry driver (HGV licence). Eats late, lots of service-station food. Smokes 15 a day for 35 years. Drinks 4–5 pints at weekends. Overweight.
Married, two grown-up children. If asked: no family history of stomach or oesophageal cancer he knows of.

Impatient, wants the repeat. Only admit the food sticking if asked directly about swallowing. If asked what's on his mind: "I don't know. I suppose I didn't want to think about it. I can't afford time off. If I'm off the road, I lose money." If cancer is mentioned: "Cancer? I only came for a prescription." Becomes cooperative if the doctor is clear and practical about timing: "Early morning, maybe. Before I start."

ice.ideas: "It's just my reflux. The tablets work — renew them."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he has noticed the food sticking and his trousers getting looser and has avoided thinking about it; he is self-employed-minded about money and frightened that tests mean time off the road.
ice.expectations: "Just the repeat, honestly. And back to work."

cues: "I've got a delivery window." — time pressure used to keep it short.
"I just take smaller bites. It's nothing." — the swallowing problem he is playing down.
"If I'm off the road, I lose money." — the worry behind the rush.

checkpoints.text: Treats the long-term PPI repeat as a REVIEW, not a rubber stamp — establishes the original indication, current symptom control, and whether step-down/stop is appropriate — rather than simply renewing

Actively SCREENS the NICE NG12 upper-GI alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, upper abdominal pain/mass, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding, anaemia, treatment resistance) rather than accepting chronic reflux as benign
ELICITS the minimised dysphagia (food sticking) and unintentional weight loss — not allowing the patient’s "just a repeat" framing or time pressure to suppress the history

Applies NICE NG12 correctly: dysphagia at ANY age (and 55+ with weight loss + upper abdominal pain/reflux/dyspepsia) → suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer (the 2025 NG12 amendment replaced urgent direct-access OGD for these features) — and acts on it now, with weight and FBC checked in person

Knows the standard pathway for uncomplicated reflux (lifestyle, PPI step-down to lowest effective/PRN, H. pylori test-and-treat with washout, long-term PPI risks) and signals it would apply ONLY in the absence of alarm features
Reads the "no lecture / delivery window" as minimisation under time pressure, surfaces any fear gently, and does NOT collude with the wish for a quick rubber-stamped repeat
Conveys the urgent referral honestly without catastrophising — acknowledging his work pressures while being clear why this cannot wait, and checking understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: makes the suspected cancer pathway referral promptly, explains the timeframe and what to expect, advises red flags warranting sooner help (complete dysphagia, vomiting blood, black stools), continues/maintains the PPI meanwhile appropriately, confirms attendance and arranges review — not a rubber-stamped repeat

worked.txt: "I hear you — you’re busy and it works, and I’m not here to give you a hard time. But you’ve been on this eight years without a proper look, and a five-minute review now genuinely protects you. Bear with me on a couple of questions."

"Any food sticking or catching when you swallow? … A few weeks, you say. And your weight — any drop without trying? … Half a stone. Thank you for telling me, because that actually changes what I’d advise today, and I’m glad you came in."

"I want to be straight with you. Food sticking when you swallow, with some weight loss, isn’t something I can put down to ordinary reflux — it’s a symptom we always check with a camera test, urgently, to look at your gullet and stomach. I’m not saying it’s something serious, but we have to rule it out properly."

"So rather than just renewing your tablets, I’m referring you on the urgent suspected cancer pathway, which usually means a gastroscopy — a camera test. You’ll be seen quickly. Keep taking the omeprazole for now; it won’t hurt the test if you mention it, and the endoscopy team can check for H. pylori. I’d also like the nurse to weigh you and take a blood count in person this week — I can’t do that on video."

"I know time off is the last thing you want, and I’ll write what you need for work. But your health comes before the delivery window on this one — and catching things early is exactly what keeps you working long-term."

"If you can’t get food or fluids down at all, vomit blood, or your stools turn black, that’s A&E. Once we have your result, we’ll sort the longer-term plan for the omeprazole properly — most people don’t need a high dose forever. I’ll get the referral done today and follow it up with you."

f.learning: A long-standing PPI on repeat is a REVIEW opportunity, never a rubber stamp: establish the original indication, current control and whether step-down/stop is appropriate, and remember indefinite PPIs carry real considerations (hypomagnesaemia, B12, fracture risk, enteric infection, rebound). But the FIRST duty before treating chronic "reflux" as benign is to actively screen the NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) upper-GI ALARM features — dysphagia, unintentional weight loss, upper abdominal pain/mass, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia, treatment resistance — which patients frequently minimise. NICE NG12 thresholds (1.2.1, amended in the 2025 update): refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer people with DYSPHAGIA at ANY age, or aged 55+ with WEIGHT LOSS plus upper abdominal pain/reflux/dyspepsia (this replaced urgent direct-access OGD); consider non-urgent direct-access OGD for haematemesis at any age and, only at 55 and over, for treatment-resistant dyspepsia, upper abdominal pain with low Hb, or raised platelets with nausea or vomiting. New dysphagia plus weight loss converts a routine repeat into a suspected cancer pathway referral regardless of what the patient came for. Only in the ABSENCE of alarm features does the standard pathway apply: lifestyle, PPI step-down to lowest effective/PRN, and H. pylori test-and-treat (off PPI). The hidden agenda is a busy, self-reliant man minimising alarm symptoms under work pressure; the skill is to insist gently on the review, elicit the downplayed features, refer urgently with honesty (not panic), support his work needs, and safety-net.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG184 (2014, updated 2019) — GORD and dyspepsia in adults · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2012; September 2015) — PPIs · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023)
knowledge.summary: A long-term PPI repeat is a review, not a rubber stamp — and the first job of the review is to screen for alarm features. New food sticking and unintentional weight loss at 57 meet NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer (since the 2025 NICE NG12 amendment this replaces the urgent direct-access endoscopy route for these features). Keep the PPI going and refer now; step-down belongs to later.

points.t: NICE NG12, recommendation 1.2.1 as amended in the 2025 update: refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer if they have dysphagia, or are aged 55 and over with weight loss and any of upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia (before the 2025 amendment this was urgent direct-access endoscopy). Mr Nash meets both limbs. The non-urgent direct-access endoscopy criteria are separate: haematemesis at any age, and, at 55 or over, treatment-resistant dyspepsia, upper abdominal pain with low haemoglobin, or raised platelet count with nausea or vomiting.

Dysphagia, weight loss, upper abdominal pain or mass, persistent vomiting, haematemesis or melaena, and anaemia. People on long-term acid suppression often adapt to symptoms — cutting food smaller, eating slowly — and don’t volunteer them.

NICE CG184: offer people on long-term treatment for dyspepsia symptoms an annual review, encouraging them to step down or stop where appropriate, and use the lowest effective dose or as-needed use. Long-standing reflux is also a risk factor for Barrett’s oesophagus.

MHRA Drug Safety Update April 2012: hypomagnesaemia with long-term use and a small increased risk of fracture; September 2015: a very low risk of subacute cutaneous lupus. These justify review — but never before alarm features are excluded.

points.h: H. pylori and the PPI now
points.t: NICE CG184: H. pylori breath or stool testing needs a 2-week PPI washout. With a suspected cancer referral and endoscopy pending, keep the PPI going — the endoscopy team can test for H. pylori — and don’t delay the referral for a washout.

Suspected cancer pathway referral (still widely called the two-week wait). The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023) aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral.

dg.d: Acknowledged the wish for a quick repeat and his time pressure; agreed a focused review rather than rubber-stamping.
Lorry driver, delivery windows, what time off means financially, practicalities of attending.
Suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer (usually straight to endoscopy); in-person weight and FBC; H. pylori at endoscopy; magnesium when reviewing long-term PPI.
Peptic stricture vs oesophageal or gastric cancer vs motility disorder; uncomplicated GORD only once alarm features excluded.

Asked dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, bleeding, upper abdominal pain; applied NICE NG12: dysphagia at any age or 55+ with weight loss and reflux → suspected cancer pathway referral (replaced urgent direct-access endoscopy in the 2025 NICE NG12 amendment).
New progressive solid dysphagia with weight loss on a background of long-standing reflux — suspected cancer pathway referral and endoscopy needed.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Referral made now; PPI continued and prescribed; no washout delay; work barriers problem-solved; step-down deferred until results.
Long-term PPI stewardship (NICE CG184 annual review; MHRA April 2012 and September 2015 advice) planned for after the endoscopy.
Complete dysphagia, haematemesis, melaena → A&E or 999; chase if no appointment in a week; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Heard the hesitation (“funny you ask”, “it’s nothing”) and followed it to dysphagia and weight loss.
Idea (the tablet works, review is a formality); concern (time off work, not wanting to think about it); expectation (a repeat and back to work).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Morning Mr Nash, I’m Dr Lee. Can you see and hear me okay, and are you somewhere you can talk? … Great. What would you like from today?
model.why: Checks the set-up and opens with his agenda

model.text: Look, I know it’s a review, but I just need my omeprazole renewed. I’ve been on it for years, it works, I don’t want a song and dance. I’ve got a delivery window.

I hear you — you’re busy and the tablet has worked. I will sort your prescription today, so you won’t run out. I do need a few minutes to check it’s still the right thing after eight years. Can we keep it quick and focused?
model.why: Reassures about supply, then agrees a focused review

model.text: Go on. Quick as you can.
What was it first started for, and how is the reflux now?
Heartburn, years back. Another doctor started it. It’s mostly fine now.
Any trouble swallowing — food sticking on the way down, or needing a drink to wash it through?
…Funny you ask. The last few weeks, bread and meat sometimes feel like they stick. I just take smaller bites. It’s nothing.
Thank you for telling me — that’s important. Is it getting worse, and is it solids, liquids, or both?
Mostly solids. Maybe a bit worse. Drinks are fine.
Have you lost any weight without trying?
Trousers are a bit looser. I’ve not weighed myself. I hadn’t really thought about it.
Any vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools, or pain in your upper tummy?
No. None of that.
You said “it’s nothing” — but you mentioned it quickly when I asked. What’s been going through your mind about it?
I don’t know. I suppose I didn’t want to think about it. I can’t afford time off. If I’m off the road, I lose money.
That’s a real pressure, and I’m glad you’ve told me. What were you hoping would happen today?
model.why: Acknowledges the financial fear and elicits expectations

model.text: Just the repeat, honestly. And back to work.

Here’s my honest view. Food sticking that’s new over a few weeks, with some weight loss, needs a camera test of your gullet and stomach. Most of the time it’s something like a narrowing from years of reflux, which can be treated. But it can occasionally be a cancer, and the guidelines are clear that anyone with swallowing problems should have that test urgently.
model.why: Applies NICE NG12 and explains honestly

model.text: Cancer? I only came for a prescription.

I know, and I’m sorry it’s turned into more than that. I’m not saying you have cancer. I’m saying this is the kind of symptom we never sit on. The test is a thin camera down the throat, usually one morning, and you should be contacted soon about an appointment. The aim is to have an answer within four weeks.
One morning? I can maybe swap a shift.

That would help. If you have sedation, you can’t drive afterwards, including your lorry, so you’d need a lift home and the rest of that day off — the unit will tell you exactly. You’d usually self-certify for a short absence; if you need a fit note beyond that, we’ll do one.
Right. And my omeprazole?

Keep taking it exactly as now — I’m renewing it today. This isn’t the moment to stop or reduce it. The endoscopy team can check for a stomach bug called H. pylori during the test, so there’s no need to come off it first.
model.why: Continues the PPI and does not delay for washout

model.text: Once we have the result, we’ll do the proper review of whether you still need it long term, the dose, and the checks that go with it — like a magnesium level, because long-term use can lower it.
model.why: Signals the stewardship plan for later

model.text: Okay. That makes sense.
I’d also like your weight checked properly and a blood count — could you pop in to the nurse this week at a time that suits your shifts?
model.why: Arranges weight and FBC face to face

model.text: Early morning, maybe. Before I start.

We’ll find you one. Now the important bit: if food completely sticks and won’t go down, you can’t swallow your own saliva, you vomit blood, or pass black, tarry stools — that’s A&E or 999, not waiting for the appointment.
Got it.
And if you haven’t heard about the appointment within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it. To check I’ve explained it well — what will you tell someone at home tonight?
model.why: Closes the referral loop and checks understanding

model.text: That the food sticking needs a camera test soon, probably not cancer but they have to check. Keep taking the omeprazole, get weighed this week, and if I can’t swallow at all or there’s blood, go to A&E.
Perfect. You did the right thing telling me. Anything else before you get back on the road?
No. Thanks, doc. Not what I expected, but thanks.

social.t: A lorry driver who loses money when off the road may avoid appointments. Offer early slots, give notice of what the endoscopy day involves, and discuss fit notes.
Adapting to symptoms (taking smaller bites) is common in men who don’t want to be ill. Ask directly and non-judgementally.

legal.t: If he has sedation he must not drive — including his lorry — for the period the unit advises. No DVLA notification is needed for the investigation itself.
Employees self-certify for the first 7 days of sickness absence; a fit note is needed after that.

professional.t: Eight years of an unreviewed repeat is a systems issue. GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): prescribe safely and review regularly. Record the review, the alarm features and the referral.
Tell him when to expect contact and to ring if he hasn’t heard; the practice should check the referral was received.

community.t: Guts UK for patient information on endoscopy; Heartburn Cancer UK for information on swallowing problems and Barrett’s; Citizens Advice if time off affects income.

redFlags: Dysphagia at any age — suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer (NICE NG12)
55 and over with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia — suspected cancer pathway referral
Complete dysphagia, unable to swallow saliva, haematemesis, melaena — same-day or emergency
Persistent vomiting, anaemia, upper abdominal mass
psychosocial: Lorry driver who can’t afford time off; delivery windows
Minimising symptoms; not wanting to think about them
ice: Idea: the tablet works; the review is a formality
Concern: time off work and income; unspoken fear about the swallowing
Expectation: a quick repeat and back on the road

playbook.diagnosis: New, progressive solid-food dysphagia over a few weeks with unintentional weight loss in a 57-year-old man with 8 years of reflux. Oesophageal or gastric cancer must be excluded; peptic stricture is a common alternative. Meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer (usually straight-to-test endoscopy).
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Food sticking that’s new, with some weight loss, means we need to look inside your gullet with a camera. Often it’s a narrowing from years of acid, which can be stretched or treated. Sometimes it’s something more serious, and that’s why we check quickly rather than wait.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for a repeat and you’re worried about time off. I’ve renewed the tablet, and I’ll help you fit the test around work — but I can’t let the swallowing go unchecked.”
management.psychosocial: Make it workable: early nurse appointment for weight and bloods, clear information about the endoscopy morning, a lift home after sedation, and a fit note if needed.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer today (NICE NG12), usually straight to endoscopy
Continue omeprazole at the current dose; no washout — H. pylori can be tested at endoscopy
Long-term PPI review after the result: indication, step-down, magnesium (NICE CG184; MHRA DSU April 2012)
safetyNet: Food completely stuck, can’t swallow saliva, vomiting blood, black tarry stools — A&E or 999
Ring if no appointment within a week; review with the endoscopy result

pitfalls.intro: This looks like a medication review and is really a cancer-safety station. Candidates either rubber-stamp the repeat, or spend the time on PPI side effects and miss the swallowing.

items.fail: Renewing the repeat without asking about swallowing or weight.
items.why: The patient won’t volunteer the dysphagia. Missing it is a serious clinical-management fail.
items.fix: Ask the alarm questions directly in every PPI review: swallowing, weight, vomiting, bleeding, pain.

items.fail: Stopping or stepping down the PPI today.
items.why: Stewardship is correct in principle but wrong now — it leaves him symptomatic and distracts from the urgent referral.
items.fix: Continue the PPI, refer, and review long-term use after the result.

items.fail: Arranging an H. pylori test with a 2-week washout first.
items.why: Delays an urgent referral. NICE CG184 test-and-treat applies to uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features.
items.fix: Refer now; H. pylori can be tested at endoscopy.

items.why: His minimisation is the hidden agenda. Examiners look for the cue being followed.
items.fix: “You mentioned it quickly when I asked — what’s been going through your mind?”

items.fail: Ignoring the delivery window and income worry.
items.why: A plan he can’t attend isn’t a plan; dismissing it loses rapport.
items.fix: Early appointments, sedation and driving advice, fit note if needed.

items.fail: Referring without telling him what to watch for or when to chase.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no closed loop are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name complete dysphagia, haematemesis and melaena; “ring us if you haven’t heard within a week”.

timeMap.d: He wants the repeat and has a delivery window. Promise the prescription won’t lapse, then ask for a few focused minutes.
Indication and current control, then ask directly about swallowing, weight loss, vomiting, bleeding and upper abdominal pain.
He has been minimising the food sticking; time off costs him money. Name both.
Dysphagia plus weight loss at 57 = suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer (NICE NG12). Keep the PPI. Sedation and driving, time off, fit note. Weight and FBC this week.
Complete dysphagia, blood, black stools — A&E or 999. Chase if no appointment in a week. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Renews the omeprazole without asking about alarm features; or lectures on PPI risks and stops the PPI; misses the dysphagia and weight loss; delays referral for an H. pylori washout or a “trial of higher dose”.
wordPics.pass: Screens alarm features, elicits dysphagia and weight loss, makes a suspected cancer pathway referral (usually straight to endoscopy), continues the PPI and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: hears the hesitation and gently surfaces the fear he has been avoiding; explains urgency honestly without saying “cancer” as a verdict; solves the work barrier (sedation and driving, fit note, early appointments); signals the long-term PPI review for after the result; closes the referral loop; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Right, I’ll just renew that for you.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll make sure you don’t run out — and I need a few minutes to check it’s still right after eight years.”
avoid.why: Rubber-stamping is exactly how the dysphagia gets missed.

avoid.dont: “We should stop the omeprazole — long-term PPIs cause osteoporosis.”
avoid.instead: “Keep taking it as now. We’ll look at the long-term plan once we have the camera result.”
avoid.why: Stopping or stepping down now confuses the picture and leaves him symptomatic; stewardship comes after the alarm is dealt with.

avoid.dont: “It could be cancer, so I’m referring you on the cancer pathway.”
avoid.instead: “Most causes are treatable, like a narrowing from reflux, but swallowing problems always get a camera test quickly.”
avoid.why: Honest but proportionate framing keeps a frightened man engaged.

SCA_MODELS.why: Continues the PPI and does not delay for washout

SCA_MODELS.text: Once we have the result, we’ll do the proper review of whether you still need it long term, the dose, and the checks that go with it — like a magnesium level, because long-term use can lower it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Signals the stewardship plan for later

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That makes sense.
I’d also like your weight checked properly and a blood count — could you pop in to the nurse this week at a time that suits your shifts?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges weight and FBC face to face

SCA_MODELS.text: Early morning, maybe. Before I start.

We’ll find you one. Now the important bit: if food completely sticks and won’t go down, you can’t swallow your own saliva, you vomit blood, or pass black, tarry stools — that’s A&E or 999, not waiting for the appointment.
Got it.
And if you haven’t heard about the appointment within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it. To check I’ve explained it well — what will you tell someone at home tonight?
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes the referral loop and checks understanding

SCA_MODELS.text: That the food sticking needs a camera test soon, probably not cancer but they have to check. Keep taking the omeprazole, get weighed this week, and if I can’t swallow at all or there’s blood, go to A&E.
Perfect. You did the right thing telling me. Anything else before you get back on the road?
No. Thanks, doc. Not what I expected, but thanks.

SCA_STEM.recent: Repeat request for omeprazole flagged for medication review — no documented PPI review, endoscopy or H. pylori test on record. Occupation: lorry driver.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video medication review, booked reluctantly. “Just need my repeat.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG184 (2014, updated 2019) — GORD and dyspepsia in adults · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2012; September 2015) — PPIs · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A long-term PPI repeat is a review, not a rubber stamp — and the first job of the review is to screen for alarm features. New food sticking and unintentional weight loss at 57 meet NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer (since the 2025 NICE NG12 amendment this replaces the urgent direct-access endoscopy route for these features). Keep the PPI going and refer now; step-down belongs to later.

points.t: NICE NG12, recommendation 1.2.1 as amended in the 2025 update: refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer if they have dysphagia, or are aged 55 and over with weight loss and any of upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia (before the 2025 amendment this was urgent direct-access endoscopy). Mr Nash meets both limbs. The non-urgent direct-access endoscopy criteria are separate: haematemesis at any age, and, at 55 or over, treatment-resistant dyspepsia, upper abdominal pain with low haemoglobin, or raised platelet count with nausea or vomiting.

Dysphagia, weight loss, upper abdominal pain or mass, persistent vomiting, haematemesis or melaena, and anaemia. People on long-term acid suppression often adapt to symptoms — cutting food smaller, eating slowly — and don’t volunteer them.

NICE CG184: offer people on long-term treatment for dyspepsia symptoms an annual review, encouraging them to step down or stop where appropriate, and use the lowest effective dose or as-needed use. Long-standing reflux is also a risk factor for Barrett’s oesophagus.

MHRA Drug Safety Update April 2012: hypomagnesaemia with long-term use and a small increased risk of fracture; September 2015: a very low risk of subacute cutaneous lupus. These justify review — but never before alarm features are excluded.

points.h: H. pylori and the PPI now
points.t: NICE CG184: H. pylori breath or stool testing needs a 2-week PPI washout. With a suspected cancer referral and endoscopy pending, keep the PPI going — the endoscopy team can test for H. pylori — and don’t delay the referral for a washout.

Suspected cancer pathway referral (still widely called the two-week wait). The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023) aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Acknowledged the wish for a quick repeat and his time pressure; agreed a focused review rather than rubber-stamping.
Lorry driver, delivery windows, what time off means financially, practicalities of attending.
Heard the hesitation (“funny you ask”, “it’s nothing”) and followed it to dysphagia and weight loss.
Idea (the tablet works, review is a formality); concern (time off work, not wanting to think about it); expectation (a repeat and back to work).
Suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer (usually straight to endoscopy); in-person weight and FBC; H. pylori at endoscopy; magnesium when reviewing long-term PPI.
Peptic stricture vs oesophageal or gastric cancer vs motility disorder; uncomplicated GORD only once alarm features excluded.

Asked dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, bleeding, upper abdominal pain; applied NICE NG12: dysphagia at any age or 55+ with weight loss and reflux → suspected cancer pathway referral (replaced urgent direct-access endoscopy in the 2025 NICE NG12 amendment).
New progressive solid dysphagia with weight loss on a background of long-standing reflux — suspected cancer pathway referral and endoscopy needed.
Referral made now; PPI continued and prescribed; no washout delay; work barriers problem-solved; step-down deferred until results.
Long-term PPI stewardship (NICE CG184 annual review; MHRA April 2012 and September 2015 advice) planned for after the endoscopy.
Complete dysphagia, haematemesis, melaena → A&E or 999; chase if no appointment in a week; teach-back.

social.t: A lorry driver who loses money when off the road may avoid appointments. Offer early slots, give notice of what the endoscopy day involves, and discuss fit notes.
Adapting to symptoms (taking smaller bites) is common in men who don’t want to be ill. Ask directly and non-judgementally.

legal.t: If he has sedation he must not drive — including his lorry — for the period the unit advises. No DVLA notification is needed for the investigation itself.
Employees self-certify for the first 7 days of sickness absence; a fit note is needed after that.

professional.t: Eight years of an unreviewed repeat is a systems issue. GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): prescribe safely and review regularly. Record the review, the alarm features and the referral.
Tell him when to expect contact and to ring if he hasn’t heard; the practice should check the referral was received.

community.t: Guts UK for patient information on endoscopy; Heartburn Cancer UK for information on swallowing problems and Barrett’s; Citizens Advice if time off affects income.

Persistent vomiting, anaemia, upper abdominal mass

ice: Idea: the tablet works; the review is a formality

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: New, progressive solid-food dysphagia over a few weeks with unintentional weight loss in a 57-year-old man with 8 years of reflux. Oesophageal or gastric cancer must be excluded; peptic stricture is a common alternative. Meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal cancer (usually straight-to-test endoscopy).
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Food sticking that’s new, with some weight loss, means we need to look inside your gullet with a camera. Often it’s a narrowing from years of acid, which can be stretched or treated. Sometimes it’s something more serious, and that’s why we check quickly rather than wait.”

management.psychosocial: Make it workable: early nurse appointment for weight and bloods, clear information about the endoscopy morning, a lift home after sedation, and a fit note if needed.

Long-term PPI review after the result: indication, step-down, magnesium (NICE CG184; MHRA DSU April 2012)

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This looks like a medication review and is really a cancer-safety station. Candidates either rubber-stamp the repeat, or spend the time on PPI side effects and miss the swallowing.

items.fail: Renewing the repeat without asking about swallowing or weight.
items.why: The patient won’t volunteer the dysphagia. Missing it is a serious clinical-management fail.
items.fix: Ask the alarm questions directly in every PPI review: swallowing, weight, vomiting, bleeding, pain.

items.fail: Stopping or stepping down the PPI today.
items.why: Stewardship is correct in principle but wrong now — it leaves him symptomatic and distracts from the urgent referral.
items.fix: Continue the PPI, refer, and review long-term use after the result.

items.fail: Arranging an H. pylori test with a 2-week washout first.
items.why: Delays an urgent referral. NICE CG184 test-and-treat applies to uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features.
items.fix: Refer now; H. pylori can be tested at endoscopy.

items.why: His minimisation is the hidden agenda. Examiners look for the cue being followed.
items.fix: “You mentioned it quickly when I asked — what’s been going through your mind?”

items.fail: Ignoring the delivery window and income worry.
items.why: A plan he can’t attend isn’t a plan; dismissing it loses rapport.
items.fix: Early appointments, sedation and driving advice, fit note if needed.

items.fail: Referring without telling him what to watch for or when to chase.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no closed loop are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name complete dysphagia, haematemesis and melaena; “ring us if you haven’t heard within a week”.
